To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
guanylyl-cyclase activating proteins (the GCAPs) modulate the light response in mouse cones.
GCAPs modulating guanylyl cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase are essential for the rapid termination of light responses and for light adaptation in mouse cones.
the GCAPs play an important role for cone phototransducion in mouse.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms underlying the modulation of cone phototransducion.
the molecular mechanisms of photoreceptor function and the molecular basis of visual adaptation.
the molecular mechanisms of light adaptation and the functional properties of phototransduction cascades in mammalian cones and rods.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
GCAPs are critical modulators of cone phototransducion, but their role is not as strong in cones as in rods.
GCAP modulation is critical for cone phototransducer modulation, but that it cannot explain the functional differences between mammalian rods and mammalian cones.
GCAPs modulates the cone phototransductive cascade, but the modulation is weaker than in rods.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
GCAPs are critical for cone function in both darkness and bright illumination and that their role in cones is different from that in rods.

The main takeaway from our work is that
GCAPs play a key role in modulating the phototransduction response in mouse cones.
GCAPs are essential modulators of mammalian cones and that their deletion severely impairs the functional properties of mammalian cone photoreceptors.

GCAPs are key players in the modulation of the phototransduction machinery in cones, but their contribution is not sufficient to fully explain the differences between the properties of rod and cone phototransductions.
